idiom_name: EF Core owned entity types (OwnsOne / OwnsMany)
implementation_notes: EF Core models the cluster with owned entity types: the owner exposes the dependents as navigation properties, OwnsOne/OwnsMany (or the [Owned] attribute) place them on the dependent side of the relationship by definition, and DbContext.ChangeTracker plus SaveChanges persist the whole graph in one transaction. Reference owned types map into the owner's table by default while collections get their own table keyed by owner key plus a local id, which mirrors aggregate semantics; a value object shared by two owners is a documented friction point - use a complex type for that.
pitfalls: Owned instances cannot be shared: assigning the same instance to two owners throws on SaveChanges; duplicate the value or model it as a complex type.
In EF Core 2.x a reference owned type could not be null unless mapped to its own table, and in EF Core 3.x its columns are always nullable - a quiet hole in required-value models.
A child removed from a collection that was never loaded cannot be recognised as an orphan, so dependents silently stay in the database.

variants.idiom_name: EF Core owned entity types (OwnsOne / OwnsMany)

variants.name: EF Core complex types (value-semantics components)
variants.implementation_notes: Complex types, introduced in EF Core 8, are the value-object counterpart of owned entity types: no hidden key, comparison by value, instances shareable across properties and mapped to columns of the containing table (table splitting) or to JSON. Use them for dependent parts that genuinely have no identity of their own; keep owned entity types when a dependent needs identity, its own table or navigations to other entities.
pitfalls: Complex types cannot contain navigations to other entities, so a dependent that references another aggregate still needs an owned entity type.
On EF Core versions before 8 the same model degrades to owned entity types with reference semantics and a hidden key.
